https://www.liverpoolecho.co.uk/travel/r.text: Ryanair flyers might be throwing away money the second they book their next holiday - and it could be avoided by making one change at the checkout. Martin Lewis’ MoneySavingExpert team claim the bargain boost can come from paying in the 'right' currency, rather than sticking with the default. It won’t always be massive money , but on some routes it’s enough to cover an airport snack or two - and for people travelling a lot, this could quickly add up. The trick is easiest to spot when you split your trip up and treat it like two separate one-ways, instead of one neat return booking. That’s because the return leg can show up priced in the currency of the country you’re flying home from. Sometimes that conversion is cheaper than Ryanair’s pound price. MSE says it’s worth a quick comparison before you hit pay. MoneySavingExpert claim the potential savings can rise with pricier flights, but it depends on the currency involved. The team wrote: "Generally speaking, the more expensive the flight, the bigger the potential saving. "In our spot check, the savings when paying in Euros were bigger than when paying in non-Euro currency (such as Polish Zloty or Hungarian Forint, which was actually more expensive to pay in than in pounds)." So Euros can be the sweet spot — while some other currencies can actually sting you. They showed a few examples online: Warsaw to London: £55.09 (GBP) vs £53.04 (Polish złoty) — 3.72% cheaper Ibiza to London: £82 (GBP) vs £77 (Euro) — 6.1% cheaper Kefalonia to London: £119 (GBP) vs £111.64 (Euro) — 6.18% cheaper Barcelona to Manchester: £25 (GBP) vs £21.64 (Euro) — 13.44% cheaper Budapest to Manchester: £63 (GBP) vs £64.34 (Hungarian Forint) — 2.13% more expensive MSE’s method is to build your return trip yourself, then compare it against Ryanair’s standard return price. They said: "Search for your outbound flight as a one-way ticket. "Then, in a separate tab or window of your browser, search for the return leg of your flight as a one-way ticket. The return flight will be in the currency of the country the flight departs from, so check what the equivalent is in pounds (use the Mastercard or Visa currency converters for the most accurate rates) then compare the total cost of both legs with that of a regular Ryanair return flight." This only properly works if your card doesn’t come with foreign transaction fees - often around 3%. People should use travel-friendly accounts, app-based banks, and certain fee-free options from traditional banks. Even if you do everything right, Ryanair may try to nudge you back into its own conversion rate. MSE’s advice is blunt - don't accept Ryanair's 'guaranteed exchange rate'. They said: "After you enter your card details, look out for a sneaky message showing the cost of your ticket in pounds (using Ryanair's exchange rate). You have to click on 'more information' to opt out and use your bank's exchange rate instead (likely to mean a much bigger saving)."

https://www.mirror.co.uk/news/world-news.text: At least one person has died and seven are in a life-threatening condition after a severe wildfire tore through cities on Croatia's coastline. On Thursday evening the wildfire broke out near the village of Lokva Rogoznica and spread quickly towards the nearby tourist town of Omis. It has been described by Croatia's fire chief Slavko Tucakovic as "one of the worst" fires in the country's history. Around 1,200 residents and tourists were evacuated while 42 patients were examined, of whom 14 were hospitalised, ten remain in intensive care units, and seven are in a life-threatening condition and on respirators, the prime minister said. Tucakovic said the firestorm burned through "everything in their path" as officials confirmed flames, fanned by strong winds, engulfed 1,000 hectares in just four hours. More than 300 firefighters were deployed overnight on Thursday, with crews sometimes forced to retreat as the fire advanced. The regional maritime authorities said 194 people, including children, were plucked from the sea and from various boats as they tried to flee the fire. Firefighters put out the blaze by Friday morning but now the country faces the devastating aftermath of the destruction the blaze left behind. Prime Minister of the Slovak Republic Robert Fico has confirmed he is supporting the situation in Croatia. Taking to X he wrote: "A short while ago, I spoke by phone with the Prime Minister of Croatia, Mr Andrej Plenković, and expressed my solidarity with him in connection with the wildfires facing this hospitable and warm-hearted country. "I also offered assistance within the limits of our capabilities. The Croatian Prime Minister informed me about the situation near the town of Omiš and the measures that have been taken. The relevant Croatian authorities and emergency services have the situation under control. Given the large number of Slovak tourists currently in Croatia, I also personally spoke with our Ambassador to Croatia, Ms Hana Kováčová. "So far, 30 Slovak tourists have contacted our Embassy in Zagreb and the Crisis Centre of the Ministry of Foreign and European Affairs of the Slovak Republic. We have no reports of any Slovak citizens being injured, although damage to their property cannot be ruled out" Croatia's Minister of Environmental Protection and Green Transition said: "I express my condolences to the family for the lost life and to all those affected by the catastrophic fire in Dalmatia. I thank the firefighters, members of the civil protection system, and volunteers who have once again demonstrated their knowledge, skills, courage, and solidarity." The Foreign Office has yet to issue any travel warnings for Brits planning a trip to Croatia.
